plan.curriculum: Mathematics 2.0, Statistics, Years 5 and 6 (VC2M5ST03, VC2M6ST03): choose appropriate displays and represent data
plan.shape: example-first: the teacher draws one column graph with every part named, then the class matches data to displays
plan.criticalFeature: match the display to the data: categories go in a column graph, small sets of numbers in a dot plot, and change over time in a line graph
decisionPoints: the choice check: which display suits a seedling's height each week?
the hinge: what is missing from this graph?
plan.anchor: ask, collect, show, tell: every investigation starts with a fair question and ends with what the data shows
plan.catchUp: Missed Session 2? Show yesterday's frequency table and point to the total before the launch.

studentTools: A ruler and a sharp pencil for every student
Printed Worksheet for every student; Extension and Supported Worksheet as needed
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
boardSetup: The week's anchor on the board: ask, collect, show, tell
Yesterday's class survey frequency table, ready to graph together

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn. Read a column graph and a dot plot, sort data to displays, draw a column graph, and fix a mistake.
resources.title: Choosing and Drawing Graphs
resources.subtitle: Match the graph to the data. Title, labels, even scale.

example.prompt: How many more students chose basketball than cricket?

items.prompt: Use the dot plot. Each dot is one player.

example.prompt: Which display suits 'temperature every hour today'?
steps: Change over time goes on a line graph.

items.prompt: Write each kind of data under the display that suits it.

example.prompt: What scale would you use if the biggest value is 12?

items.prompt: Draw a column graph of how students get to school. Give it a title, label both axes and use an even scale.
items.answer: Title, both axes labelled, an even scale (steps of 1 or 2), columns 7, 12, 5 and 3.

example.prompt: Is a line graph good for favourite pets?
steps: A line between categories means nothing.

items.prompt: Mia drew a line graph of the class's favourite fruits. Find her mistake and fix it.
work: Apple, banana, grapes, orange along the bottom.
I joined the points with a line.
items.answer: Fruits are categories, not times, so a joining line means nothing. Draw a column graph.

items.prompt: A graph's scale goes 0, 2, 4, 8, 10. What is wrong?
items.explain: From 4 to 8 jumps 4, but the other steps jump 2, so the columns would look the wrong size.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option. A double column graph, reading a line graph between points, and designing your own display, with worked examples.
resources.title: Extension: Graph Detective
resources.subtitle: Compare, read between the lines, then design.

example.prompt: Which sport did 5A like more than 5B?
steps: Find where the 5A column is taller.

parts.prompt: Which sport did both classes choose equally?
Which class liked netball more, and by how many?

example.prompt: About what was the temperature at 11 am?

items.prompt: Use the line graph of the temperature on a spring day.
Could you use the line graph to estimate the temperature at 2 pm? Explain.
items.answer: Yes: about 24 degrees, halfway between 25 at 1 pm and 23 at 3 pm, because the temperature changes smoothly.

example.prompt: Plan a display for 'hours of sleep each night this week'.
steps: The data changes over the week: time.

items.prompt: Choose your own question for the class to answer. Say which display you would use and why, then sketch it with made-up data.
items.answer: Check: the display matches the data (categories: column; numbers: dot plot; time: line), with a title, labels and an even scale.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: For students who need more guidance: graph parts to label, values to read with a ruler, and a word bank.
resources.title: Graphs: Step by Step
resources.subtitle: Every graph needs a title, labels and an even scale.

example.prompt: What does a graph's title tell you?
steps: It says what the graph shows.

items.prompt: Match each part of a graph to its job.
rows: Says what the graph is about
Numbers going up in equal steps
answers: Says what the graph is about
Numbers going up in equal steps

steps: Put a ruler across the top of the Dog column.

slides.notes: Session 3 of our statistics week: today we choose and draw graphs that suit our data.

Before you start, put boards, markers, a ruler and a pencil on every desk, and keep yesterday's class frequency table on the board. Print the Worksheet for everyone, and a few copies of the Extension and the Supported Worksheet.

slides.title: Read a point
prompts: What are the coordinates of Q?

beats: SAY: Let's warm up with the Cartesian plane from last week.
ASK: What are the coordinates of Q?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: (-2, -3)
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal and move straight on.
Less -> say left or right, then up or down, from the origin together. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's negative 2, negative 3: left 2 and down 3.
Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing (2, 3) with no signs.
Fix: ask which side of the origin Q is, and they add the signs.
notes.prep: Review of Week 2 coordinates (the request named the focus). Keep the review under 6 minutes.

beats: ASK: How big is the reflex angle?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 235
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal and move straight on.
Less -> trace the full turn: 360 take away the inside angle. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's 235 degrees, because 360 take away 125 is 235.
Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 55, from 180.
Fix: trace all the way round, and they redo it from 360.

beats: ASK: How do you write three eighths as a decimal?
30 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 0.375
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then on to Fluency.
Less -> find one eighth first, 0.125, then times 3. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: One eighth is 0.125, so three eighths is 0.375. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 0.38 or 3.8.
Fix: halve a half three times to find one eighth,
0.125, and they multiply by 3.

slides.title: Subtract with the written method: 3 digits

beats: SAY: Now for some written subtraction.
Line up the places, and always start with the ones.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
30 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 437
SCAN boards for the regrouped columns.
80%+ -> reveal, then the next one.
Less -> model the first column together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 437.
Tick it or fix it, and check every step.
trap: taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in every column.
Fix: ask "Is the top digit big enough?", and they regroup and redo it.
notes.prep: Subtraction fluency: 3 digits, then 4, then 5. Keep the whole block under 6 minutes.

slides.title: Subtract with the written method: 4 digits

beats: SAY: Now it's 4 digits.
It's the same method, just one more column.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
45 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 5 365
SCAN boards for the regrouped columns.
80%+ -> reveal, then the next one.
Less -> model the first column together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 5 365.
Tick it or fix it, and check every step.
trap: taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in every column.
Fix: ask "Is the top digit big enough?", and they regroup and redo it.

slides.title: Subtract with the written method: 5 digits

beats: SAY: Now it's 5 digits.
It's the same method, just one more column.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 33 557
SCAN boards for the regrouped columns.
80%+ -> reveal, then the learning intention.
Less -> model the first column together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 33 557.
Tick it or fix it, and check every step.
trap: taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in every column.
Fix: ask "Is the top digit big enough?", and they regroup and redo it.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to choose and draw a graph that suits our data.
successCriteria: I can name the parts of a graph: title, labels and scale.
I can draw a column graph with an even scale.
I can explain which display suits the data and why.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: We've asked and collected.
Today we show our data in a graph,
so people can see it at a glance.
SAY: Let's read our I can statements together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: The first one is where we start,
and the second one is our big goal today.
notes.prep: SC1 naming the parts is reachable for everyone; SC2 drawing the column graph is the core; SC3 choosing the display is the stretch and the exit evidence.

slides.title: See it at a glance
slides.prompt: Which way of travelling is most common?

beats: POINT to the graph.
SAY: Here's the data from yesterday's I Do, shown as a column graph.
ASK: Which way of travelling is most common, and how could you tell so quickly?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: car: it has the tallest column
SCAN boards for car.
80%+ -> cold call one student: How did the graph help?
Less -> point to each column top and read the scale together. Re-ask.
SAY: Car is most common: its column is the tallest.
A graph lets people see the answer at a glance, and today we'll draw one.
trap: reading the scale wrongly.
Fix: lay a ruler across the column top, and they read it again.
notes.prep: The launch comes after the LI: why we graph data. Under 4 minutes.

slides.meaning: The numbers up the side of a graph, going up in equal steps.

notes.answer: the numbers up the side, in equal steps
beats: POINT to the word.
SAY: This word is scale. Say it with me: scale.
SAY: The scale is the numbers up the side of a graph.
They must go up in equal steps, or the columns look the wrong size.
ASK: What step does this scale go up in?
5 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 2
trap: counting the gridlines instead of reading the numbers.
Fix: read the numbers on the scale aloud, and they find the step.
notes.prep: An even scale is the most common error in student graphs.

slides.title: Draw a column graph
steps: Write a title that says what it shows.
Choose a scale with equal steps.
Draw each column up to its value.

beats: MODEL the title and labels.
SAY: Let me draw this graph from our pets table.
First the title, Our pets, then I label both axes.
MODEL the scale.
SAY: The biggest value is 9, so I'll count up in ones to 10.
Equal steps keep every column honest.
ASK: How tall should the Fish column be?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 3
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Fish is 3. Every column reaches exactly its value,
and the title, labels and scale tell the reader what they're looking at.
trap: starting the columns above zero.
Fix: trace from the bottom line up, and they redraw it.
notes.stretch: What scale would you use if the biggest value were 45?
notes.help: Use the grid squares: one square for each student.
notes.prep: Title, labels, an even scale, then the columns. SC1 and SC2.

rows: Small sets of numbers, like pets at home
Change over time, like temperature each day

beats: SAY: Different data suits different displays.
Categories, like favourite sport, go in a column graph.
SAY: A small set of numbers,
like how many pets you have, suits a dot plot.
And when something changes over time, we use a line graph.
ASK: Which display would you use for the temperature every hour today?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: a line graph
trap: choosing a column graph for everything.
Fix: ask: is it categories, numbers or time? and they choose again.
notes.stretch: Think of data that could suit two different displays.
notes.help: Ask: is it words, numbers, or time?
notes.prep: Matching display to data is the critical feature and SC3.

slides.title: A seedling's height each week
slides.prompt: Which display suits this data? Point to A, B or C

options.misconception: uses a column graph for change over time
uses a dot plot, which loses the order of the weeks

beats: SAY: A seedling is measured every week.
Think about what kind of data that is.
ASK: Which display suits a seedling's height each week?
15 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: pointing to C
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then cold call one student: Why not A?
Less -> ask: does it change over time? Point to the line graph row. Re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: It's C, the line graph. The height changes over time,
and the line shows the growth from week to week.
trap: pointing to A.
Fix: ask what happens between week 1 and week 2, and they choose again.
notes.prep: First decision point: matching the display to the data. A column graph here is the common error.

slides.title: Which display?
slides.ask: Which display suits this data? Write column, dot or line.
slides.pivot: ask: categories, a few numbers, or change over time?
slides.followUp: cold call one board: Why does that display suit it?

items.text: Goals each player scored this season, 0 to 6

items.say: A line graph: your height changes over time.

say: Write column, dot or line on your board.
trap: choosing column graph for data over time.
Fix: ask whether it changes over time, and they choose again.
notes.stretch: Give a title and axis labels for one of them.
notes.help: Use the display table on the board.
notes.prep: Guided practice across all three displays. SC3.

slides.title: What is missing from this graph?

beats: SAY: This one is just for you.
Look at this graph carefully.
ASK: What two things is this graph missing?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: a title and labels on the axes
SCAN every board, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then Your turn.
Less -> hold up our pets graph beside it and compare. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's missing a title and axis labels.
We can't tell what 12 means, or what the days are measuring.
Tick it or fix it.
trap: saying it needs more columns.
Fix: ask what the numbers on the side measure, and they look again.
notes.prep: The hinge before independent drawing. Anyone who names only one starts on the Supported Worksheet with the teacher.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.task: Read, choose and draw graphs on your worksheet.

beats: POINT to the steps.
SAY: Read each question carefully, solve it carefully, then check your answers.
SAY: If you finish, the Extension is your early finisher option.
Let's read the steps together. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE and ask: What does your scale go up in? Is every step equal?
TIME: 20 minutes. Stop everyone once at 10 minutes to share a strategy.
trap: an uneven scale.
Fix: count the steps aloud, and they redraw the scale.
notes.stretch: Extension: a double column graph, a line graph and your own display.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: graph parts to label and columns to read with a ruler.
notes.prep: Independent practice: read two graphs, sort displays, draw a column graph and reason about mistakes. The sheet is evidence for SC2 and SC3.

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: This table shows a puppy's mass each month. Which display would you use, and why?

notes.answer: a line graph: the mass changes over time
beats: SAY: Here's the last one. Work it out on your own board.
ASK: Which display would you use for the puppy's mass each month, and why?
30 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: a line graph: the mass changes over time
RECORD who chooses a column graph or gives no reason.
They start tomorrow's check with the teacher.
trap: choosing a column graph.
Fix: none now. Record the name for tomorrow.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC3 with SC2 in the reason: a new context, change over time.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Tell your partner how you choose a display.

notes.answer: open - listen for categories column, a few numbers dot plot, time line graph
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can statements together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can
choose and draw a graph that suits the data?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit board.
A thumb up with 'column graph' on the board matters most.
ASK: How do you choose which display to use?
20 sec. Cue: Partner A first. You have 20 seconds. Go.
EXPECT: categories column, a few numbers dot plot, time line graph
notes.prep: Read the self-assessment beside the exit evidence. Tomorrow we read graphs and tell what they show.
